Empirical Research Plan: Market Reactions to New Information  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Panel event‐study / difference-in-differences (DID) that stacks many information shocks.  

Why appropriate  
• The research question is about the *instant* price impact of identifiable news events (earnings announcements, macro releases, policy decisions).  
• Each event generates an “information shock” whose exact *calendar time* is known, while its *content* (positive, negative, or neutral surprise) is unanticipated.  
• We observe security-level daily (or intraday, if available) returns for long pre- and post-event windows, so we can compare:  
 (a) treated security-days in a short window around the shock vs.  
 (b) the same securities in non-event days *and* other securities that experience no shock at the same time.  
• A stacked event-study DID with security and calendar-date fixed effects removes permanent security traits and aggregate market moves, delivering a causal estimate of the news shock.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Setting used below: quarterly corporate earnings announcements (you could replicate the design for macro or policy events).  

• Treatment variable  
 T_isτ = 1 if security i is within event window τ ∈ {-1, 0, +1} relative to its own earnings-announcement day; 0 otherwise.  
 We will break T into event-time dummies (τ = –5,…,+5) for dynamic effects.  

• Control observations  
 – *Within-firm, different times:* same security outside the ±5-day window.  
 – *Cross-section, same day:* securities with no announcement that day.  
 The two dimensions combined in a two-way-FE regression form the counterfactual.  

• Treatment timing / event date  
 Event date = firm-specific earnings announcement date drawn from Compustat or IBES; day 0 = announcement day.  

• Running variable / cutoff  
 Not an RDD, so none.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends / common shocks.  
 Absent the event, treated and control returns would evolve similarly over very short horizons once we partial out firm and day fixed effects.  
 Plausibility: high for ±5-day windows; both groups are exposed to the same overall market (captured by date FE).  

A2. No anticipatory trading within the defined pre-window.  
 Investors cannot perfectly predict surprises, so abnormal returns should be zero in days –5 to –1.  
 Checkable via pre-trend coefficients.  

A3. Surprise component exogenous to short-run firm value.  
 Conditional on expected earnings, the *surprise* is random. We proxy surprises with standardized forecast errors from IBES.  

A4. No interference (SUTVA).  
 One firm’s earnings surprise doesn’t mechanically change another’s in the same short window (reasonable, except for same-industry spillovers—can be handled by clustering or excluding).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Anticipation or leakage (violates A2)  
 • Test: coefficients on τ = –5…–1 should be ≈0.  
 • Fix: shrink event window (e.g., [0,+1]) or drop firms with known history of leaks.  

T2. Concurrent confounding events (mergers, macro news on same day)  
 • Control: include security-specific news dummies (M&A, dividend, guidance) and an indicator for major macro announcements on that date; or drop event-days with overlapping firm-specific news.  
 • Date fixed effects already absorb common macro shocks.  

T3. Non-random timing of announcements (firms choose day with good/bad market conditions)  
 • Include day-of-week × month fixed effects.  
 • Use *surprise* magnitude as treatment intensity; timing choice does not predict the surprise conditional on controls.  
 • Robustness: IV using SEC’s filing‐deadline rules (e.g., 10-Q deadline) that force announcement timing.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast manipulation
library(fixest)         # high-dim FE regressions
library(lmtest)         # coeftest for robust SEs
library(sandwich)       # clustered SEs

# 1. Load and merge -------------------------------------------------
# Assume three CSVs: prices.csv, earnings.csv, ibes.csv
prices   <- fread("prices.csv")     # id, date, ret, mkt_ret, size, bm
earn     <- fread("earnings.csv")   # id, ann_date
ibes     <- fread("ibes.csv")       # id, ann_date, eps_act, eps_est

# 2. Prepare panel --------------------------------------------------
# daily abnormal return using CAPM with rolling beta (simple version: market-adjusted return)
prices[, abret := ret - mkt_ret]   

# merge announcement info
setkey(prices, id, date); setkey(earn, id, ann_date)
panel <- earn[prices, roll = Inf]   # merge all possible rows
panel <- merge(panel, ibes, by.x = c("id","ann_date"), by.y = c("id","ann_date"), all.x=TRUE)

# 3. Event-time variables ------------------------------------------
panel[, ev_day := as.integer(date - ann_date)]
panel[, treat := ifelse(ev_day >= -5 & ev_day <= 5, 1L, 0L)]

# create event-time dummies
for(k in -5:5){
  panel[, paste0("tau",k) := as.integer(ev_day==k)]
}

# earnings surprise (scaled)
panel[, surprise := (eps_act - eps_est)/abs(eps_est)]

# 4. Main stacked DID / event study --------------------------------
# baseline window (-1,0,+1) pooled
panel[, treat_3day := as.integer(ev_day %in% c(-1,0,1))]

est <- feols(abret ~ treat_3day | id + date,
             data = panel, cluster = ~id)

summary(est)

# 5. Dynamic specification -----------------------------------------
dyn <- feols(abret ~ tau-5+tau-4+tau-3+tau-2+tau-1+tau0+tau1+tau2+tau3+tau4+tau5 |
               id + date,
             data = panel, cluster = ~id)
iplot(dyn)   # pre-trend check & impulse response

# 6. Robustness: placebo pseudo-events ------------------------------
# randomly assign pseudo dates within firm
set.seed(123)
placebo <- panel[, .SD[sample(.N,1)], by = id]   # one random date per firm
placebo[, placebo_ev := 1L]

panel <- merge(panel, placebo[, .(id, date, placebo_ev)],
               by = c("id","date"), all.x = TRUE)
panel[is.na(placebo_ev), placebo_ev := 0L]

placebo_est <- feols(abret ~ placebo_ev | id + date,
                     data = panel, cluster = ~id)
summary(placebo_est)
```
Notes  
• Use industry-date two-way clustering if worried about correlation in shocks.  
• For IV robustness: replace treat_3day with 2SLS using “deadline within 1 day” as an instrument.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory (semi-strong market efficiency) predicts that *unexpected* positive news is impounded almost immediately.  
• Magnitude: A one-standard-deviation positive earnings surprise should raise cumulative abnormal return (CAR) in [0,+1] by roughly +3 % (based on classic Jones (1991) and more recent estimates).  
• Dynamics: Day 0 jump, little drift; insignificant pre-trends.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID / event study)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Parallel pre-trends (tested with τ < 0) .................... 1  
C2: No simultaneous confounders (controls, FE) ................. 0.5  
C3: Exogeneity of treatment timing/content (surprise) .......... 0.5  
C4: Correct inference (clustered, many events) ................. 1  
C5: No interference/spillovers ................................ 0.5  
Total (out of 5) = 3.5 – solid but still requires robustness work.
